Often the problem with maths education is described as being it's lack of real world application (i.e. taxes). I think that while this is an important skill in itself, this answer misses the mark somewhat. Almost all of the maths taught in school consists of tools and techniques required to solve maths problems. Thus, the creativity, intuition and resilience required to solve genuinely interesting and fun maths problems is almost always ommitted, often only being taught in optional clubs for people who have already decided that they are a ‘maths person’. I think that not only is this type of maths (focusing on problem-solving) more engaging for students; the general problem solving skills gained are much more transferable to everyday life than techniques for solving a specific type of equation. These techniques must be learned, but to centre the entire curriculum around them seems absurd, and I think wrongly convinces many people that maths is boring and devoid of creativity, which couldn’t be further from the truth. Show less Read more Like 117 Dislike Reply 12 replies Hide replies 12 replies @vtravels24_7 1 month ago I go to School Of Humanity, it is an online middle and highs school where we don’t have exams but are instead graded on our projects, which are solutions to real world projects. We also don’t have normal subjects but instead have an interdisciplinary approach by learning through real world challenges. This way we get to learn and work on a project we are interested in as well as learn how to create actual solutions to today problems, like apps, bussines proposals, websites, 3d prototypes etc.. Show less Read more Like 57 Dislike Reply 10 replies Hide replies 10 replies @ritazamoraamengual6883 1 month ago I don’t know, thinking about a class that could teaxh us how to invest sounds like something that would help us adapt to the already existing capitalist system, but doesn’t really think beyond how to redistribute wealth. I used to work as an arts teacher in a school and moved towards working in museums and have been long outside the teaching world. I do acknowledge the problems with teaching (beeing funding one of its principal problems in Spain particularly) but, for example, i do remember very inspiring teachers in school and mostly in uni who shared they’re knowledge acquired over years of studying in that particular field and it was eye opening for me. Like I think I benefited from listening to people who know a lot about something -especially teachers who d”ditched” the curriculum a bit and talked about their own research i.e. books they had written about a specific subject, or what conclusions they drew from their work as researchers at uni-. But maybe that interest was already there and I just leaned into it, who knows. Show less Read more Like 22 Dislike Reply 8 replies Hide replies 8 replies @silvialogan9226 1 month ago If I was in charge of the Education system, I would inform the teachers never to yell at students if they fail tests or assignments especially if they tried their best and studied and made them withdraw from the program. I know because it happened to me when I was in high school and college. A math teacher yelled at me in high school because I failed two math tests the second term and discouraged me from taking math and accused me of being lazy and my marks slipping. In college, a Chef Instructor yelled at me because I failed the Demo 2 mid-term test and stated rudely that my skills were poor and yelled at me for not doing the canapes properly and overcooking the lamb and undercooking the Brussel Sprouts. He even called me stupid and said that I could not do things. That is why I hate cooking and I prefer baking instead. Show less Read more Like 22 Dislike Reply 2 replies Hide replies 2 replies @aphroditesroses3 1 month ago i don’t think the education system is responsible for five year old being glued to tablets. that’s a parent choice not a teachers choice, you could be the best teacher but if the parents aren’t parenting at home then that will have a knock on effect on the child’s performance in the classroom Show less Read more Like 130 Dislike Reply 12 replies Hide replies 12 replies @b_the_biologist 1 month ago Very interesting. I am a teacher in South Africa working in a high school with children who are from communities and environments filled with violence, addiction and not very good role models. Teenage pregnancies and absent parents with little to no resources are the norm. In a context like this I think school provides an escape and a sense of hope for these children. School and teachers that have an education beyond high school provides a world for these learners to dream bigger but for some of them they are only at school because the government say they must be. I am sharing this because my ideal for education has always been to empower learners and to help them think critically but as a new teacher seeing the reality of the country I live in I realise that sometimes transforming education as a whole would be impossible but helping one child to feel loved, seen and seen is the true purpose. Thank you for your videos, Jade! Always helps me think about these important questions.
